components.name: Error Pages
components.description: When a page can't be shown, say what happened in plain words and give people a way forward, inside the usual header, navigation and footer. Send the real HTTP status with the page, so browsers, search engines and monitoring see the error too.
notes: 404, Not Found: The address is wrong or the page moved. Offer the home page and the site's search, or its main list.

500, Something Went Wrong: The problem is on your end, so say so. Offer to try again, and say who to contact if it keeps happening. Serve it as a plain file the web server can send even when the app is down.
503, Down for Maintenance: Say when it will be back, in AP style: "until 6 p.m. Eastern." The web server sends this one too.

403, No Access: The user is signed in, but the page isn't for them. Say who it's for, not what's on it, how to get access if they should have it and where to go instead. Someone who isn't signed in yet should get the Sign In box instead.
Keep codes and details out of the heading. The number can go in small text at the bottom, for anyone reporting it; stack traces and server messages belong in the logs.

components.name: ID Tap / NFC
components.description: For checking people in or looking them up with their CMU ID card, such as at a desk, a workshop or an exam room. An NFC card reader acts as a keyboard: it types the card's number into whatever has focus, and is assumed to end it with a carriage return (Enter), which submits the form. So the target holds a hidden text field, and the number arrives as an ordinary form post.
notes: Ready on load: when it's the only ID tap on the page, the field takes focus when the page loads, so the reader works without a click. The target says Ready while the field has focus, and to select it when it doesn't, so a tap never goes nowhere. Selecting anywhere on the target focuses the field, and so does sending the form.

A tap-only page: add data-cmu-tap="keep" on a kiosk or check-in page, and the field also takes focus back whenever nothing else has it. On a page where something else should have focus first, use data-cmu-tap="click", and the field waits to be selected.

Say who it found: after each tap, put the person's name in cmu-tap-result, so the person at the desk can catch a wrong card. It takes Ready's place, so the target doesn't move.
Keep the number private: the field is never shown, and the app should clear it after each tap and never log card numbers.

Open Graph tags describe the page for apps that generate previews. Add them to the page's <head>. This example is for an equipment reservation page:

Most pages are website: a home page, a service or help page, a form or an app's pages. Checkers such as LinkedIn's report “No author found” and “No publication date found” for them, which is fine: those fields are for articles.

A page that's dated and written by someone is an article: a news story, a blog post, an announcement or a recap of an event. Give it the type, its date and its author, so previews can show when it was published:
notes: Keep the title specific: Use the page's name followed by the site's name, as in its <title>.

Give the time and time zone: Write the date as above, with the offset from UTC, -05:00 in winter and -04:00 in summer.
Add the modified time only after a real change, such as a correction, not every time the page is published.

components.name: Sorting
components.description: Items to put in order, such as the steps of a task: a numbered list with up and down arrow buttons on each item, which cmu-app.js adds. Each button names its item for screen readers, focus stays on the item as it moves and its new place is read out. Put a hidden <input> in each item; it moves with the item, and the form sends the new order. Without the script, the list keeps its first order. In React, Svelte or Vue, which own the list, see the Framework tab: render the buttons yourself and handle the cmu-sort-move event.
examples:

React.text: The list is React's, so render the buttons yourself and handle cmu-sort-move: cancel it and reorder your state. The kit adds no buttons and moves nothing; it still says where the item went and keeps focus on it.

Svelte.text: The list is Svelte's, so render the buttons yourself and handle cmu-sort-move: cancel it and reorder your state. The kit adds no buttons and moves nothing; it still says where the item went and keeps focus on it.
Svelte.code:
{#each steps as step, i (step)}
  1. {step}
    2. {/each}

Vue.text: The list is Vue's, so render the buttons yourself and handle cmu-sort-move: cancel it and reorder your state. The kit adds no buttons and moves nothing; it still says where the item went and keeps focus on it.

Rails.text: Rails renders the list, and the kit adds the buttons and moves the items; the hidden fields send the new order as order[]. With Turbo, a page restored from its cache already has the buttons, and the kit doesn't add them twice.
Rails.code:
<% @steps.each do |step| %>
  1. <%= step.title %><%= hidden_field_tag "order[]", step.id %>
    2. <% end %>

components.name: Tables With Actions
components.description: The bulk bar sits on top of a table.alternate: the selection count, then actions for the selected rows. Its height is fixed, so buttons appearing don't push the table down. Each row gets one button, the next thing to do, and a ⋯ menu with the rest; a row with nothing else to do gets no menu.
notes: One button per row: solid for something missing (Upload Syllabus), outlined when it's there (Replace Syllabus), at one fixed width and the height of a two-line button so rows stay even.

The ⋯ menu (cmu-row-menu) holds the row's other actions, in the bulk bar's words: a button for each, or a link for one that goes somewhere. Name the ⋯ button for screen readers ("More actions for 15-112 A") and give it a matching title. cmu-app.js opens it, one at a time; a click elsewhere or Escape closes it.

Something to open, such as a file, gets a plain link in a column of its own before the actions, with its type after it: "View [PDF]." Keep the row's title plain text. Hide the column's header with sr-only and name what the link opens ("Syllabus"); the actions column's hidden header is "Actions."

Selection: the app's script keeps the count current ("No sections selected" when there are none), adds cmu-has-selection to it when anything is selected and shows each bulk button only when it applies to a selected row, with how many: "Upload Syllabus (2)." Try it above.
Checkbox cells: the label fills the cell, so the whole cell is the click target.
Sorting: put data-sort-key on the header and a button.cmu-sort inside it; set aria-sort on the sorted column. For filtering, see Filters.
cmu-fit shrinks a column to its content. num (on th and td) right-aligns numbers.
Keep labels together with  , so "a" never ends a line inside a button.

conventions.heading: Classes
conventions.text:
- The template comes first. See what it already has on the Components page (the ones labeled Template), and use its classes as they are: btn, btn small, ghost, cta, table.alternate, sidebar, sr-only. The kit never copies the template's rules or values, and adds a class only for what the template doesn't already do.
- Everything in the kit starts with cmu-: classes, custom properties (--cmu-red) and JavaScript hooks (data-cmu-copy). Variations use a double hyphen (cmu-pill--green). Give your own classes your own prefix, never cmu-.

conventions.heading: AP Style
conventions.text:
Follow The Associated Press Stylebook for grammar, punctuation, numbers and dates. CMU names AP style as its preferred standard in its Brand Standards writing guide. The kit's docs follow it too. The rules that come up most on web pages:
- No comma before the last item in a simple series: "red, white and blue." Add one only when the sentence would be unclear without it.
- Dates: Abbreviate the month with a date, "Jan. 11," but not alone or with only a year: "January 2027." Spell out March, April, May, June and July. Ranges take a hyphen with no spaces: "Dec. 7-18," "2-3 p.m.," "2026-27."
- Times: "9 a.m.," "2:30 p.m.," "noon" and "midnight." Drop ":00."
- Numbers: spell out one through nine and use figures for 10 and up, except for measurements, percentages, ages, dates and times, which always take figures: "three columns," "a 768px screen."
- Keep "a" with its noun. If a lone "a" would end a line, join it to the next word with  , as in a camera. Don't use nonbreaking spaces to force whole sentences onto one line.

conventions.heading: CMU Names and Terms
conventions.text: Follow the university's naming and capitalization guidance:

conventions.heading: Headings
conventions.text:
- Capitalize the principal words, as AP does for the titles of works: headings, buttons, navigation and labels. That includes every word of four or more letters, such as "With" and "From," and the first and last word: "Upload Your Syllabus." Use sentence case for prose: "Upload your syllabus before classes start."
- A question used as a heading is a heading, as in an FAQ: “Who Can See the Syllabi?” Its answer is prose, in sentence case.
- Write a tagline or slogan in sentence case, like a sentence: this site's is “Tailored to the CMU web template,” under its name. Headings and headlines stay in Title Case, as on the university's own pages.
- Leave periods off headings and hero titles. Use normal punctuation in full sentences.
- Put the important words first. People read the first two or three words of a heading, link or list item and move on: "Syllabus Due Dates for Spring," not "Information About When Spring Syllabi Are Due."
- Choose heading levels by what they contain, never by how big they look, and don't skip a level. Screen reader users move through a page by its headings, so the headings alone should outline the page.
- Read the page as a task. Can someone scan the headings, find the main action and tell what happens after they select it?

conventions.heading: Buttons and Links
conventions.text:
The template gives buttons, calls to action and ordinary links different visual weight. Match that weight with words that say what happens next: start with a verb and name the task.
Too Vague
"Options," "Syllabus Upload" or "Learn More" makes people guess what comes next.
Ready to Use
"See the Options," "Upload Syllabus" or "Read the Instructor Guide."
A link goes somewhere; a button does something. Use a link (<a>) even when it looks like a button, and a <button> for an action even when it looks like a link: screen readers and keyboards treat them differently. These examples lead to real kit pages:
Install the Kit
The main action: a btn link, in Title Case. It can lead to a page on this site, your app, its sign-in or a request form in another system.
Explore the Content Blocks
A next step on this site: a call to action (cta), in Title Case. Put one at the end of the section, after the information that supports it.
Browse the code on GitHub
Another site: an ordinary external link, in sentence case. A link gets cta or external, never both.
- A button and a call to action side by side go in one paragraph, button first; the kit spaces them as in a hero.
- Buttons line up on the left, under what they act on, with the main one first. The one exception is the question card: back on the left, forward on the right.
- A thin rule goes over buttons that finish a whole box: a dialog, a framed panel or a question card. The kit draws it. Buttons loose in a page, such as a form's Submit or a call-to-action row, get no rule.
- Link a home page by its folder, never index.html: A site's home is ./ from its own pages and ../ from a page one folder down, and another site's is its folder's address, such as https://www.cmu.edu/syllabusregistry/. The address stays short and stays right if the site moves. Use ./, not /, which skips past a site that isn't at the server's root.
- Never write "click here." A link should make sense on its own, because people scan links and screen readers list them: "Read the Instructor Guide," not "Click here for the guide." Give links on the same page different words, so that list doesn't read "Read More, Read More, Read More."
- Label special destinations. After a link that requires sign-in, add [login required] as plain text outside the link. After a file link, add its type, such as [PDF]. These labels tell people what to expect before they select the link.
- Omit [login required] when the link text already makes it clear, as in "Sign In to See Your Courses." Use only one label: a PDF that also requires sign-in gets [login required] for people who aren't signed in, and [PDF] once they are.

conventions.heading: Heroes
conventions.text:
Say what the site or app does, then give it two next steps: a button for the main action and a "Get Started" call to action. That second link jumps to the first section below, also headed Get Started. Here's the pattern from the kit's home page:
The title names the purpose, the lead says who it's for and the button names the action. The screenshot shows what people can expect. Use the hero component to build your own.

conventions.heading: Instructions
conventions.text:
Write to the person doing the task, in the active voice: "Upload your syllabus," not "Syllabi may be uploaded by instructors." Name each control exactly as it appears on screen, and put steps in the order people follow them, one main action in each.
Hard to Follow
"Users should navigate to the appropriate course and use the queue functionality to submit a request for assistance."
Easy to Follow
- Sign in and select My Courses.
- Choose the course you need help with.
- Select Join the Queue and describe your question.
Don't point by color, shape or position alone: "Select Join the Queue," not "Click the red button on the right." People using a screen reader, a phone or a zoomed-in screen may not see it where you do. Say "select," not "click," since not everyone uses a mouse.
Write a path through menus with the breadcrumb arrow (›, ›), not the greater-than sign: “Add Content › Block › Text Block,” with each name as it appears on screen. It's the same mark the template puts between breadcrumbs.

conventions.heading: Messages
conventions.text:
"An error occurred" leaves the reader stuck. An error message names the problem and offers a way forward; a success message confirms what changed. Say it in words, not color alone. Each of these sample flash messages starts with what happened and reads the same without the red or green.
Your syllabus wasn't uploaded. Choose a PDF file and try again.
Your syllabus was uploaded. Students can now find it in the course list.

conventions.heading: Colors
conventions.text:
Keep a site to one or two colors, and use each for the same job everywhere, such as red for every sign-in box. Color goes on whole bands and boxes, not on text, and the template sets its text color to match. Two tools do it: the template's color classes for bands and boxes, and the kit's color variables for your own stylesheet. A band can also take a background pattern, the globe or the plaid. A color class goes on a sidebar box or on a whole grid; boxes inside a grid stay white. Add invert for white text on every color except grey and gold, which take dark text. Under each class is the brand color it is, from brand.cmu.edu, or "template" where cmu.edu uses its own shade, a little darker so white text on it stays readable. See also the kit's color variables. red, darkgrey, grey, blue, teal, green, darkgreen, gold, and the kit's cmu-lightgrey
…

Color Variables Use these custom properties in your own stylesheet instead of copying the values, so every site moves together if they change. Each comes from one of three places: - Brand: CMU's official colors, from brand.cmu.edu, such as Carnegie Red and the Tartan palette's threads. - Template: the colors cmu.edu's template draws on the web. Some are brand colors exactly; others are a shade darker so text on them stays readable, such as its green, close to Green Thread. The template's own color classes are on the color classes. - Kit: pale tints for backgrounds and dark shades for small text on them, such as the green of a "Syllabus Available" pill. They aren't brand colors: no brand color is pale enough for a background behind text, or dark enough for small text on a tint, in every hue. Use them only for those jobs, and a brand or template color for anything large, such as a band or a bar.

conventions.heading: Images
conventions.text:
- Alt text describes what the picture shows, in a sentence or less, without "Image of" or "Photo of": screen readers already say it's an image. For a screenshot, describe what the reader should notice, not every detail.
- A decorative image gets empty alt text (alt=""), so screen readers skip it. A linked image's alt text says where the link goes.
- Captions add what alt text doesn't: who's in the photo, where and when, and the credit. Don't repeat the caption in the alt text. See Photo Captions and Credits.
- A photo set as a background, such as the template's hero, gets role="img" and an aria-label describing it, since it has no alt.
- Keep words out of images. Put them in the page, where they can be resized, translated and read aloud.
- Videos require checked captions and a title on the frame. See Videos.

conventions.heading: Accessibility
conventions.text:
Under the university's Digital Accessibility Policy, CMU websites and web apps must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA. The template and the kit's components give you a start; the words, headings, images and links are yours. The Digital Accessibility Office has guidance, training and help, and the CMU Web team's accessibility best practices cover Cascade sites.
